properties.decision:
Anthony's word, 2026-07-30, after asking for the open requirements to be strongly scrutinised: an unaccepted requirement that is not value-adding and only causes confusion should be retired as "considered, but not accepted" rather than carried. NINE of twenty-six went. All are `dropped`, not deleted: the capture was real and the reasoning is worth keeping, so each keeps its full statement and a snapshot of its final state on the timeline (`epoch:prune-proposed`).

DROPPED AS NOT VALUE-ADDING (7).

`req:drift-rolls-up-to-a-score` and `req:framework-is-chosen-not-defaulted` — both record a DOUBT rather than a need, and say so in their own names: "probably NOT from a single scalar" and "a framework registry is probably the wrong fix". A requirement that argues against its own mechanism is a Decision wearing the wrong hat. The live fact inside the second (`Project.domain` is written and never read) survives inside `req:defaults-do-not-assert`.

`req:friction-has-a-baseline` and `req:friction-has-a-severity-bar` — measuring reflow2's own usability against a baseline, and a threshold at which friction becomes scheduled work. Both are backlog hygiene dressed as product requirements: the answer to unconverted friction reports is to act on them, not to model them.

`req:context-is-a-modelled-quantity` — `cap:bounded-reads` already answers the acute version, where a read that would not fit says so and names what it withheld. What remained was design-time estimation, which the requirement's own text calls the weak half.

`req:blocking-is-partial` — freezing drifted work while the rest proceeds. Nobody has been hurt by the all-or-nothing gate; speculative.

`req:adopt-says-how-much-it-got` — REDUNDANT with `req:coverage-visible`, which is accepted and delivered by `cap:coverage`.

FOLDED INTO `req:defaults-do-not-assert` (2). `req:edge-defaults-do-not-assert` and `req:functional-vocabulary-computes` restate one rule — node defaults, edge defaults and declared-but-unread vocabulary are the same defect: THE SCHEMA MUST NOT DECLARE WHAT NOTHING READS OR CHECKS. Their measured evidence is preserved inside the surviving requirement rather than lost with them.

A CORRECTION MADE DURING EXECUTION, kept on the record because the reasoning that produced it was wrong in an instructive way. `req:supporting-is-not-conflict` was proposed for folding as the third member, on the grounds that it had exactly ONE edge and was "an orphan in all but name". That single edge was an incoming SATISFIES from `cap:supporting-is-not-conflict`, which is `realized` — the contradiction detector already reads `alignment`. So the requirement was not an orphan; it was DELIVERED, and its status had simply never moved off `proposed`. It is now `accepted`. Low edge count was read as low value, and for a requirement that has been built, edge count is exactly backwards: a delivered requirement needs only one edge, the one from the thing that delivered it.

NOT TOUCHED, and worth recording why. The 2026-07-28 planning cluster — `req:epochs-can-be-planned`, `req:plans-move-honestly`, `req:version-combination-is-an-object`, `req:graph-indexes-snapshots` — are Anthony's own ideas, quoting him directly (the Black-Scholes analogy for plan volatility, "in systems engineering, I think this would be 2 views of the same system"). They are structurally disconnected, but that means CAPTURED AND NEVER WIRED, not low value. The fix for those is to wire them, not to retire them. `req:assumptions-are-first-class` (ordinary risk practice) and `req:correspondence-rules-are-stateable` (ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010) likewise stand.
properties.name: Nine proposed requirements considered and not accepted — seven dropped, two folded into one rule
properties.rationale:
The prompt was his: "if some of them are not value added and just cause confusion, then we don't have to do them — we can retire them as considered, but not accepted."

The test applied to each was whether the requirement would change what anyone BUILDS. A requirement that records a doubt does not; it records that a mechanism looked wrong, which is a Decision. A requirement that restates one already accepted does not; it splits one thread in two. A requirement that describes how the project should manage itself does not; it is process. What survived is everything with a code citation, a real incident, or a standing external practice behind it.

TWO SIGNALS AGREED ON FOUR, and the fifth disagreement is the useful one. `req:framework-is-chosen-not-defaulted`, `req:functional-vocabulary-computes`, `req:friction-has-a-baseline` and `req:friction-has-a-severity-bar` each sat in a `disconnected_community` island AND on the retire list on their merits. But the same check listed four of Anthony's own ideas as islands, and `req:supporting-is-not-conflict` — nearly edgeless — turned out to be delivered. So structural isolation is evidence about WIRING and never about worth, in either direction: it over-accuses parked captures and it under-accuses delivered work whose thread is short. Checking the one edge before dropping it is what caught that, and the check cost one call.

DROPPED, NOT DELETED, which is the retire-from-design skill's central distinction. These were genuinely considered — several were found by measurement. Deleting them would erase why the surviving rules are shaped as they are, and would let the same captures be re-made next quarter by someone who could not see they had been weighed. `dropped` also stops them raising `unsatisfied_requirement`, so the open list means what it says again.
